extracted.intended_audience: researchers and academics (especially those new to peer reviewing journal articles)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for conducting effective peer reviews of journal manuscripts, covering whether to accept an invitation, how to read and assess papers (contribution, rigour, style), writing the review, recommendation categories, submission and re-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should (1) aid in the vetting and selection of research for publication, ensuring that the best work is taken forward; and (2) provide suggestions for improving articles that go through review, raising the general quality of published research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep these twin aims in mind when evaluating a manuscript — both gatekeeping (fit and quality) and constructive improvement are goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the type of peer review being used
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can be single-blind (reviewers know authors, authors don't know reviewers), double-blind (neither party knows the other's identity), open (identities known and reviews sometimes published), or post-publication (reviews after publication, often open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware how the review model affects confidentiality, tone and whether reviews may be published; single-blind is still most common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to accept the invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting, consider: Do I have the appropriate expertise? Do I have any conflict of interest? Do I have the time to complete the review by the requested deadline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure of expertise, discuss scope with the editor (you might still assess specific aspects). Declare any potential conflicts to the editor. If unable to meet the deadline, inform the editor promptly and, where possible, suggest alternative reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest include anything that might impede your ability to give an unbiased assessment of the article or its author(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have a potential conflict, tell the editor before proceeding. Refer to COPE guidelines for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and follow journal-specific reviewer guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals issue peer review guidelines or a recommended structure for reviews when you accept an invitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read any provided guidance carefully and adapt your review to the journal’s requirements; ask the handling editor if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: First reading — form an overall impression
rubrics_metrics.description: On first reading, aim to form an overall impression and understanding of the article, noting recent related work, the article’s statement of purpose, and the likely impact on the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make high-level notes on contribution and fit for the journal to guide deeper evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second reading — detailed evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a detailed, objective reading focusing on key aspects (contribution, rigour, style/structure) to produce a rounded evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes tied to specific passages and examples that you can cite in the review to substantiate critiques and suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to the discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the article makes a contribution to the discipline, how significant that contribution is, whether the authors explain its importance adequately, and whether the article is a good fit for the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider novelty, scope, and potential impact; comment on fit for the target journal and advise editors on significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic rigour and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the methodology or argument is sound; whether interpretations of data or sources are reasonable; whether there is sufficient evidence to substantiate claims; whether appropriate references are cited and fairly assessed; and whether information (data, formulae, quotations, references, tables and figures) is accurate and correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific methodological flaws or unsupported claims, suggest missing essential references, and flag factual/data errors with precise examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: References and engagement with literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the appropriate references are cited, whether any essential references are missing, and whether those cited are assessed fairly by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend specific citations where necessary and note if the literature review misrepresents or omits key work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style, structure and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the article’s structure is clear and well organised; whether the aims are introduced and contextualised effectively; whether conclusions are summarised effectively; whether language is clear and correct; and whether the abstract accurately presents the aims, argument and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to sections that need reorganization, unclear prose, or an inaccurate/unclear abstract; suggest concrete edits where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a structured, evidence-based review
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reviewers summarise their overall thoughts in opening paragraphs and then provide detailed substantiation and revision suggestions with examples in the remainder of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a concise summary of the paper and your overall assessment, then list major and minor points, supported with page/line references or quotations to help authors and editors act on the feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate essential vs optional revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly indicate which suggested changes are essential to publication and which are desirable but non-essential, to help editors and authors prioritise work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For minor revisions, specify essential fixes (e.g. language edits, small experiments, citations) and separate optional improvements; for major revisions, explain why large changes are necessary and whether the article could be sound after such work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation categories (editorial routes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide one of the editor's possible recommendations: (1) Accept without revision; (2) Minor revisions needed; (3) Major revisions needed; (4) Inappropriate (reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the guidance in the categories: 'Accept' is rare; 'Minor revisions' includes small edits, small additional experiments, a few new citations, or tweaks to interpretation; 'Major revisions' includes major structural reorganization, additional experiments, reworking flawed analyses, or addressing a new topic; 'Inappropriate' applies if the article is unsound in principle or methodology or lacks significant contribution — give objective evidence in support of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear reasons and evidence for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If recommending rejection or noting major problems, give objective reasons and evidence so the editor understands your concerns and the author can learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about methodological or conceptual flaws rather than offering only broad negative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit review by the agreed deadline and via the correct channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit your review to the handling editor by the agreed deadline, often through online systems such as ScholarOne or Editorial Manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow submission instructions provided by the editor; if you cannot meet the deadline, notify the editorial office promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-reviewing revised manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to review a revised manuscript, compare the revised version with your initial review to ensure proposed changes have been made successfully and to suggest additional changes if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most manuscripts go through one or two revision stages; explicitly note whether earlier requested changes were addressed and whether remaining issues persist.
